source_document: Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., NIPS 2017)
description: Question and ideal-answer pairs for evaluating retrieval-augmented QA over the Transformer paper. Ideal answers are paraphrased and self-contained.

data.question: What is the Transformer and how does it differ from earlier sequence transduction models?
data.ideal_answer: The Transformer is a sequence transduction architecture that relies entirely on attention mechanisms. Unlike earlier dominant models, it removes recurrence and convolutions altogether. It keeps the encoder-decoder layout but builds both halves from stacked self-attention and point-wise feed-forward layers, which makes it far more parallelizable and quicker to train.

data.question: Why do the authors argue that recurrent models are a bottleneck?
data.ideal_answer: Recurrent models compute hidden states step by step along the symbol positions, each depending on the previous state. This inherent sequentiality prevents parallelization within a training example, which matters most for long sequences because memory limits restrict how many examples can be batched together.

data.question: How is the Transformer encoder structured?
data.ideal_answer: The encoder is a stack of N = 6 identical layers. Each layer has two sub-layers: a multi-head self-attention mechanism and a simple position-wise fully connected feed-forward network. A residual connection followed by layer normalization wraps each sub-layer, so the output is LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)). All sub-layers and embedding layers output vectors of dimension 512.

data.question: How does the decoder differ from the encoder?
data.ideal_answer: The decoder also has six identical layers, but each layer adds a third sub-layer that performs multi-head attention over the encoder output. Its self-attention sub-layer is masked so a position cannot attend to later positions. Residual connections and layer normalization are used around every sub-layer, as in the encoder.

data.question: How does the model preserve the auto-regressive property during decoding?
data.ideal_answer: Decoder self-attention is masked by setting the softmax inputs that correspond to illegal (future) connections to negative infinity. Combined with the fact that output embeddings are shifted right by one position, this guarantees that the prediction for position i depends only on known outputs at positions before i.

data.question: How is an attention function defined in the paper?
data.ideal_answer: An attention function maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the query, keys, values and output are all vectors. The output is a weighted sum of the values, and each value's weight comes from a compatibility function between the query and the corresponding key.

data.question: What is scaled dot-product attention and what is its formula?
data.ideal_answer: It computes dot products of the query with all keys, divides them by the square root of the key dimension d_k, applies softmax to get weights, and uses those weights to combine the values. In matrix form: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V.

data.question: Why are the dot products scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k)?
data.ideal_answer: For large d_k the dot products grow large in magnitude. If query and key components are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance d_k. Large values push the softmax into saturated regions with extremely small gradients, so dividing by sqrt(d_k) keeps the values in a range where learning works well.

data.question: How do additive attention and dot-product attention compare?
data.ideal_answer: Additive attention scores compatibility with a feed-forward network that has a single hidden layer. The two have similar theoretical complexity, but dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice because it can use highly optimized matrix multiplication. Without scaling, additive attention outperforms dot-product attention for larger d_k, which is why the paper adds the 1/sqrt(d_k) factor.

data.question: How does multi-head attention work and what settings does the base model use?
data.ideal_answer: Queries, keys and values are linearly projected h times with different learned projections to d_k, d_k and d_v dimensions. Attention runs in parallel on each projected version, the resulting d_v-dimensional outputs are concatenated, and a final projection W^O produces the output. The base model uses h = 8 heads with d_k = d_v = d_model / h = 64, so total computation is similar to single-head attention at full dimensionality.

data.question: What advantage does multi-head attention provide over a single attention head?
data.ideal_answer: It lets the model jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. With a single head, averaging inhibits this. It also counteracts the reduced effective resolution that comes from averaging attention-weighted positions.

data.question: In what three ways does the Transformer use multi-head attention?
data.ideal_answer: First, encoder-decoder attention, where queries come from the previous decoder layer and keys and values come from the encoder output, so every decoder position can attend over the whole input. Second, encoder self-attention, where queries, keys and values all come from the previous encoder layer. Third, masked decoder self-attention, where each position attends only to positions up to and including itself.

source.section: 3.2.3 Applications of Attention in our Model

data.question: What does the position-wise feed-forward network look like?
data.ideal_answer: It is applied to each position separately and identically and consists of two linear transformations with a ReLU in between: FFN(x) = max(0, xW1 + b1)W2 + b2. Input and output dimension is 512 and the inner layer has dimension 2048. Parameters are shared across positions but differ from layer to layer; it can also be seen as two convolutions with kernel size 1.

data.question: How are embeddings and the output softmax handled?
data.ideal_answer: Learned embeddings convert input and output tokens to d_model-dimensional vectors, and a learned linear transformation plus softmax turns decoder output into next-token probabilities. The same weight matrix is shared between the two embedding layers and the pre-softmax linear transformation, and in the embedding layers the weights are multiplied by sqrt(d_model).

data.question: How does the Transformer encode token order?
data.ideal_answer: Because the model has no recurrence or convolution, positional encodings of dimension d_model are added to the input embeddings at the bottom of the encoder and decoder stacks. The paper uses sinusoids: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d_model)) and PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^(2i/d_model)), with wavelengths forming a geometric progression from 2π to 10000·2π.

data.question: Why did the authors choose sinusoidal positional encodings over learned ones?
data.ideal_answer: They hypothesized sinusoids make it easy for the model to attend by relative position, since for any fixed offset k the encoding at pos+k is a linear function of the encoding at pos. They may also let the model extrapolate to longer sequences than seen in training. Experiments with learned positional embeddings gave nearly identical results.

data.question: What three criteria motivate the use of self-attention?
data.ideal_answer: The total computational complexity per layer, the amount of computation that can be parallelized (measured by the minimum number of sequential operations), and the path length between long-range dependencies in the network. Shorter paths between any input and output positions make long-range dependencies easier to learn.

data.question: How do self-attention, recurrent, convolutional and restricted self-attention layers compare in complexity, sequential operations and path length?
data.ideal_answer: Self-attention: O(n^2 * d) per layer, O(1) sequential operations, O(1) maximum path length. Recurrent: O(n * d^2), O(n), O(n). Convolutional: O(k * n * d^2), O(1), O(log_k(n)). Restricted self-attention with neighborhood r: O(r * n * d), O(1), O(n/r). Here n is sequence length, d is representation dimension and k is kernel size.

data.question: Under what condition is a self-attention layer faster than a recurrent layer?
data.ideal_answer: When the sequence length n is smaller than the representation dimensionality d. This is the usual case for sentence representations in state-of-the-art machine translation, such as word-piece and byte-pair encodings. For very long sequences, self-attention can be restricted to a neighborhood of size r, at the cost of a longer maximum path length of O(n/r).

data.question: How do convolutional layers compare with self-attention for connecting distant positions?
data.ideal_answer: A single convolutional layer with kernel width k < n does not connect all input-output pairs, so a stack of O(n/k) layers (contiguous kernels) or O(log_k(n)) layers (dilated convolutions) is needed, lengthening the longest paths. Convolutions are also more expensive than recurrent layers by a factor of k. In ConvS2S the cost of relating two positions grows linearly with distance and in ByteNet logarithmically, whereas the Transformer needs a constant number of operations.

data.question: What datasets, tokenization and batching were used for training the translation models?
data.ideal_answer: English-German used WMT 2014 with about 4.5 million sentence pairs and byte-pair encoding with a shared vocabulary of about 37,000 tokens. English-French used the much larger WMT 2014 set of 36 million sentences with a 32,000 word-piece vocabulary. Sentence pairs were batched by approximate length, with each batch holding roughly 25,000 source tokens and 25,000 target tokens.

data.question: What hardware and training time were needed for the base and big models?
data.ideal_answer: Both were trained on one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. The base model took about 0.4 seconds per step and was trained for 100,000 steps, roughly 12 hours. The big model took about 1.0 second per step and was trained for 300,000 steps, roughly 3.5 days.

data.question: What optimizer and learning rate schedule were used?
data.ideal_answer: The Adam optimizer with beta1 = 0.9, beta2 = 0.98 and epsilon = 1e-9. The learning rate is d_model^-0.5 * min(step^-0.5, step * warmup_steps^-1.5), which increases linearly for the first 4000 warmup steps and then decays proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number.

data.question: Which regularization techniques are applied and with what values?
data.ideal_answer: Residual dropout is applied to the output of each sub-layer before it is added to the sub-layer input and normalized, and also to the sums of embeddings and positional encodings; the base model uses a rate of 0.1. Label smoothing with value 0.1 is also used. The big English-to-German model uses dropout 0.3, while the big English-to-French model used 0.1.

data.question: What is the effect of label smoothing?
data.ideal_answer: It hurts perplexity because the model learns to be more unsure, but it improves accuracy and BLEU score.

data.question: What BLEU score did the Transformer achieve on WMT 2014 English-to-German?
data.ideal_answer: The big Transformer reached 28.4 BLEU, a new state of the art that beat the best previous results, including ensembles, by more than 2 BLEU. Even the base model (27.3 BLEU) surpassed all previously published models and ensembles at a fraction of the training cost. The big model trained for 3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs.

data.question: What BLEU score did the Transformer achieve on English-to-French and at what cost?
data.ideal_answer: Table 2 and the abstract report 41.8 BLEU for the big model, a new single-model state of the art, after 3.5 days on eight GPUs and at less than a quarter of the training cost of the previous best model. The base model scored 38.1. Note that the running text of Section 6.1 states 41.0, which is inconsistent with the table and abstract.

data.question: How much training compute did the Transformer models require compared with prior systems?
data.ideal_answer: The base model needed about 3.3e18 FLOPs and the big model about 2.3e19 FLOPs. By comparison, ConvS2S used about 9.6e18 (EN-DE) and 1.5e20 (EN-FR), GNMT + RL about 2.3e19 and 1.4e20, and the ensembles were far higher, for example 1.2e21 FLOPs for the ConvS2S ensemble on English-French.

data.question: How were training FLOPs estimated?
data.ideal_answer: By multiplying the training time, the number of GPUs used, and an estimate of the sustained single-precision floating-point capacity of each GPU. The paper used 2.8, 3.7, 6.0 and 9.5 TFLOPS for the K80, K40, M40 and P100 respectively.

data.question: What decoding and checkpoint settings were used for the translation results?
data.ideal_answer: Base models used a single model made by averaging the last 5 checkpoints (written at 10-minute intervals), and big models averaged the last 20 checkpoints. Decoding used beam search with beam size 4 and length penalty alpha = 0.6, with maximum output length set to input length + 50 but terminating early when possible. These values were chosen on the development set.

data.question: What did the ablations show about the number of attention heads?
data.ideal_answer: Holding computation constant while varying heads and key/value dimensions, single-head attention was about 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting (24.9 vs 25.8 on the dev set), and quality also dropped when there were too many heads (for example 25.4 BLEU with 32 heads).

data.question: What happens when the attention key dimension d_k is reduced?
data.ideal_answer: Reducing d_k hurts model quality. The authors take this to suggest that determining compatibility between queries and keys is not easy and that a more sophisticated compatibility function than dot product might be beneficial.

data.question: What did the ablations show about model size and dropout?
data.ideal_answer: As expected, bigger models performed better, and dropout was very helpful in avoiding over-fitting. For instance, removing dropout (0.0) dropped dev BLEU to 24.6 versus 25.8 for the base setting.

data.question: How do learned positional embeddings compare with sinusoidal encodings?
data.ideal_answer: Replacing the sinusoidal encoding with learned positional embeddings gave nearly identical results: 25.7 BLEU versus 25.8 for the base model on the English-to-German development set, with the same perplexity of 4.92.

data.question: How large are the base and big models and how do they score on the dev set?
data.ideal_answer: The base model has about 65 million parameters and scores 25.8 BLEU on newstest2013 (perplexity 4.92). The big model uses d_model = 1024, d_ff = 4096, 16 heads and dropout 0.3, has about 213 million parameters and scores 26.4 BLEU (perplexity 4.33), trained for 300K steps.

data.question: How was the Transformer applied to English constituency parsing?
data.ideal_answer: A 4-layer Transformer with d_model = 1024 was trained on the Wall Street Journal portion of the Penn Treebank (about 40K sentences) and also in a semi-supervised setting with about 17M sentences, using 16K and 32K token vocabularies respectively. Only a small number of experiments tuned dropout, learning rates and beam size; other parameters stayed as in the translation base model. Inference used maximum output length of input + 300, beam size 21 and alpha = 0.3.

data.question: How well did the Transformer perform on parsing compared with other parsers?
data.ideal_answer: It scored 91.3 F1 in the WSJ-only setting and 92.7 F1 in the semi-supervised setting on WSJ section 23. It outperformed the Berkeley Parser even when trained only on 40K sentences, unlike earlier RNN sequence-to-sequence models. The paper says it beats all previously reported models except the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar (93.3 F1); note that Table 4 also lists a multi-task result of 93.0 from Luong et al., which is higher than 92.7.

data.question: What does the attention visualization for the word 'making' show?
data.ideal_answer: In layer 5 of 6 of the encoder self-attention, many heads attend from 'making' to a distant dependency, completing the phrase 'making...more difficult'. Different colors represent different heads.

data.question: What do the attention heads in Figure 4 appear to do?
data.ideal_answer: Two heads in layer 5 of 6 (heads 5 and 6) appear to be involved in anaphora resolution. For the word 'its', their attention is very sharp, linking it to the antecedent 'Law' and to 'application'.

data.question: What does Figure 5 illustrate about the behavior of different attention heads?
data.ideal_answer: It shows two different heads from encoder self-attention at layer 5 of 6 whose behavior seems related to the structure of the sentence. The heads clearly learned to perform different tasks, supporting the claim that self-attention can yield more interpretable models.

data.question: Who contributed which ideas to the Transformer according to the author notes?
data.ideal_answer: Jakob Uszkoreit proposed replacing RNNs with self-attention and started evaluating the idea. Ashish Vaswani, with Illia Polosukhin, designed and implemented the first Transformer models. Noam Shazeer proposed scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention and the parameter-free position representation. Niki Parmar designed, implemented, tuned and evaluated many model variants. Llion Jones built the initial codebase and worked on efficient inference and visualizations. Lukasz Kaiser and Aidan Gomez designed and implemented tensor2tensor, which replaced the earlier codebase.

data.question: Where can the code used to train and evaluate the models be found?
data.ideal_answer: In the tensor2tensor repository on GitHub (github.com/tensorflow/tensor2tensor).

data.question: What future work do the authors propose?
data.ideal_answer: They plan to apply attention-based models to other tasks, extend the Transformer to input and output modalities beyond text, investigate local or restricted attention to handle large inputs and outputs such as images, audio and video, and make generation less sequential.

data.question: Why can the Transformer learn long-range dependencies more easily than ConvS2S or ByteNet, and what trade-off does it make?
data.ideal_answer: The number of operations needed to relate two arbitrary positions grows linearly with distance for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet, whereas in the Transformer it is constant, giving a maximum path length of O(1). The trade-off is reduced effective resolution from averaging attention-weighted positions, which the paper counteracts with multi-head attention.

data.question: How does the cost-efficiency of the big Transformer compare with the ConvS2S ensemble on English-to-French?
data.ideal_answer: The big Transformer used about 2.3e19 FLOPs and scored 41.8 BLEU, while the ConvS2S ensemble used about 1.2e21 FLOPs for 41.29 BLEU. The Transformer therefore achieved higher BLEU with roughly 50 times less training compute.

data.question: What accuracy does the Transformer achieve on ImageNet classification?
data.ideal_answer: The paper does not report any ImageNet results. It only mentions images as a possible future modality for the Transformer.

data.question: How does the paper's BERT pre-training objective work?
data.ideal_answer: The paper does not discuss BERT or any pre-training objective; it focuses on supervised machine translation and constituency parsing.

data.question: Does the paper use rotary position embeddings?
data.ideal_answer: No. It uses fixed sinusoidal positional encodings and compares them with learned positional embeddings, but does not mention rotary embeddings.
